newsitem.title: USA: CHESS-Kasparov should not have resigned game, experts say.
newsitem.headline: CHESS-Kasparov should not have resigned game, experts say.

text.p: World chess champion Garry Kasparov made a remarkable and rare oversight in the second game of his re-match with the supercomputer Deep Blue and should not have resigned, grandmasters said on Tuesday.
The realisation and controversy overshadowed the start of the third game of the contest on Tuesday and was a reminder to human players that their emotions can be a handicap in clashes with machines.

Several leading grandmasters admitted that they too had initially missed the continuation that would have saved the day for Kasparov. It was left to an untitled player in an Internet chat room to unlock the problem. Deep Blue's programmers also said it had not calculated the moves during the game.

"I think he was deluded into thinking that he was completely lost because the flow of the game was completely against him," English grandmaster Daniel King told Reuters. "In a way he was psyched out by the computer's performance."
Grandmasters intensely debated how the strongest player in chess history overlooked a sequence of moves that would have forced a draw on Sunday and maintained his lead in the match.

Instead, the 34-year-old Russian resigned the position after the IBM system's 45th move and the match was tied at one win each. Kasparov defeated the machine on Saturday in the first game of the $1.1 million six-game match.
"It played so brilliantly I didn't think to check it," Kasparov was quoted as saying by associates.
Chess experts, almost without exception described Sunday's game as the best performance ever by a computer, likening it to the style of leading grandmasters.
Kasparov, playing with the black pieces, was forced by Deep Blue to defend for almost four hours and looked tired and demoralised.
"The computer has an advantage, it does not have this body of emotions. We humans get depressed," grandmaster Yasser Seirawan of the United States said. "The computer doesn't get depressed."

Subsequent analysis showed that Kasparov could have played a series of moves to force what is known in chess as "perpetual check" -- one player repeatedly attacking his opponent's king, ensuring none of his other pieces can make further moves and thus a draw is the only outcome.
The analysis began within hours of the game ending in "chat rooms" run by the Internet Chess Club. Surprisingly, it was an untitled player who first suggested the drawing sequence.

Internet Chess Club director Gregory Belmont said that Michigan University philosphy professor Tim McGrew suggested a queen move threatening the computer's king and a critical defensive rook move for Kasparov. He said nine grandmasters and 10 international masters joined the discussion and came to the conclusion that the sequence was sound.
"People cooperate in a way that microprocessors don't," Belmont said. Deep Blue has 32 processors connected with each other by switches and can examine hundreds of millions of positions per second.

Just how bad a mistake it was for Kasparov, world champion since 1985, would depend on how it affected him psychologically and whether he recovered with a positive result on Tuesday, expert observers said.

"I have heard of grandmasters resigning in winning positions even because they did not see the key idea," International Master and match commentator Mike Valvo told Reuters. "The psychological impact is unestimable, it's just enormous."
The third game opened slowly on Tuesday, much the same as in the first when Kasparov also had the white pieces and the advantage of the opening move, similar to having serve in tennis.

He chose an English Opening in which white seeks a positional advantage and avoids tactical complications. After 35 moves, Kasparov appeared to have an advantage after sacrificing a pawn to set up a potential assault on the black king.
